hints: Focus on what type of C-C bond is present in the monomer ethene compared to the polymer chain.
Remember ethene contains a C=C double bond, while poly(ethene) contains only C-C single bonds after addition polymerisation.
Link bond order to length and strength, remembering that higher bond order means shorter and stronger bonds.
walkthrough:
**Identify the bonding in ethene**

Think of ethene as a small alkene with a double bond between the carbons. That double bond is made of one sigma and one pi bond.

$$\text{CH}_2=\text{CH}_2 \text{ contains C=C}$$

**Identify the bonding in poly(ethene)**

During addition polymerisation the pi bond breaks and each carbon forms a new single sigma bond to join the chain. So the backbone is all single bonds.

$$n\text{CH}_2=\text{CH}_2 \rightarrow \text{-[CH}_2\text{-CH}_2\text{-]}_n \text{ contains C-C}$$

**Compare single vs double bonds**

A double bond pulls the atoms closer and holds them more tightly than a single bond. So going from C=C to C-C means the bond gets longer and weaker.

Bond order up = shorter + stronger, bond order down = longer + weaker.

options.A: Longer is correct, but stronger is not. A single bond cannot be stronger than a double bond between the same atoms because it has lost the pi bond contribution.
options.B: Correct. Ethene has C=C double bonds, poly(ethene) has C-C single bonds. Single bonds are longer and weaker than double bonds.
options.C: This describes the opposite change. Shorter and stronger would be true if we went from single to double, but polymerisation goes from double to single.
options.D: Weaker is correct, but shorter is not. Weaker bonds are almost always longer, not shorter, because the atoms are held less tightly together.
